data.name: Wargame: Airland Battle
data.detailed_description:
2 SIDES, 12 NATIONS, 750 UNITS: THE STRATEGY GAME REFERENCE IS BACK!

Richer, more beautiful and more accessible, Wargame AirLand Battle is the sequel to the explosive real-time strategy game Wargame European Escalation!

1985. After several months of tension between NATO and the Warsaw Pact, an incident in the North Sea suddenly sets the world on fire, starting an all-out war.
Command the entire military resources of the period, and plunge into the heart of a new dynamic campaign! With the arrival of air forces, select from a phenomenal array of 750 units (including tanks, planes, helicopters, and infantry) to build your army. Engage in spectacular battles with unmatched strategic depth, on huge battlefields as large as 150km², powered by a new graphics engine.

Impressive in solo play, Wargame AirLand Battle is even more engaging online. The game features ultra-complete multiplayer modes, where up to 20 players do battle simultaneously!

reviews.review:
Wargame: AirLand Battle is a demanding real-time strategy experience that takes the Cold War and turns it into a massive combined-arms battlefield where preparation is every bit as important as direct combat. Developed and published by Eugen Systems, it abandons traditional RTS conventions such as constructing bases and rapidly producing units in favor of commanding predetermined military forces across enormous maps. The result is a game that initially feels intimidating but becomes increasingly rewarding once its reconnaissance, logistics, positioning, and unit-counter systems begin to make sense.

Set in an alternate 1985, the conflict imagines tensions between NATO and the Warsaw Pact escalating into full-scale warfare after an incident in the North Sea. The scenario provides an excellent foundation for the enormous selection of period military hardware. Twelve nations and around 750 units are represented, including infantry, tanks, armored transports, reconnaissance vehicles, artillery, helicopters, anti-aircraft systems, and fixed-wing aircraft. This variety is more than cosmetic because vehicles and weapons possess different battlefield roles, capabilities, ranges, and vulnerabilities.

Building an effective force is consequently one of the game's most interesting strategic elements. Simply filling a deck with powerful tanks is rarely enough. Heavy armor can dominate exposed ground but becomes vulnerable when advancing without reconnaissance, infantry, anti-air protection, or logistical support. Helicopters can punish isolated units but are extremely vulnerable to suitable air defenses. Aircraft can rapidly change the course of a battle, yet sending an expensive plane directly into enemy anti-air coverage is an excellent way to lose valuable resources. Every category has a purpose, encouraging combined-arms tactics instead of dependence on a single dominant unit.

The introduction of aircraft is especially important. Fighters, bombers, and ground-attack aircraft expand the battlefield beyond what was offered in Wargame: European Escalation. Air support can destroy important targets or rescue a struggling frontline, but aircraft require careful timing and knowledge of enemy defenses. This produces an enjoyable relationship between reconnaissance, air superiority, ground forces, and anti-air systems. Successful attacks often feel like actual coordinated operations rather than simple groups of units being ordered toward the enemy.

The enormous battlefields complement this philosophy. Maps can reach roughly 150 square kilometers, leaving plenty of room for maneuvering, flanking, defensive positions, and long-range engagements. Forests and settlements provide opportunities for concealed infantry and ambushes, while open terrain can become extremely dangerous for inadequately supported forces. Roads allow units to travel quickly but can also create predictable movement routes. Scouting therefore becomes essential. Knowing what lies ahead can be more valuable than having another expensive combat vehicle.

Logistics add another layer of complexity. Units consume ammunition and fuel, meaning an army cannot necessarily remain effective indefinitely without support. Supply vehicles and logistical planning become important during prolonged engagements. This encourages players to consider not only whether they can capture a position but whether they can maintain the forces required to hold it. Combined with morale, suppression, reconnaissance, weapon ranges, and positioning, these mechanics create battles where careful preparation frequently defeats reckless aggression.

The dynamic campaign gives solo players a larger strategic framework rather than limiting the experience to isolated skirmishes. Managing military resources and fighting tactical engagements provides considerable depth, although newcomers should expect a steep learning curve. There is a lot of information to absorb, particularly when hundreds of available units have different statistics and specialized purposes. Players accustomed to simpler RTS games may initially struggle with the amount of knowledge required, but learning why an operation failed is a major part of the appeal.

Multiplayer pushes these mechanics even further, supporting battles involving as many as 20 players. Human opponents make reconnaissance and adaptability particularly important because their intentions are far less predictable. Large matches can become spectacular conflicts involving artillery bombardments, armored advances, helicopter attacks, air strikes, and desperate defensive actions across several fronts. Online play also rewards communication because coordinated teams can combine specialized forces much more effectively than players acting independently.

Visually, the game inevitably shows its age, but its presentation remains impressive for the scale being represented. The ability to move between a broad strategic perspective and much closer views of individual units gives battles an impressive sense of scope. Tanks, aircraft, explosions, missile launches, and artillery exchanges provide plenty of spectacle without distracting from the tactical information required to command effectively. The relatively modest system requirements also make it accessible to considerably older hardware.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable rather than Verified. The game can function on the handheld and its default graphics configuration performs well, but there are compromises. Some interface text can be small, occasional prompts may display mouse, keyboard, or non-Steam Deck controller icons, and text entry can require manually opening the virtual keyboard. All functionality is accessible with the default controller configuration, but the interface and strategic precision naturally feel more comfortable with a traditional mouse and keyboard. An active internet connection is also required for single-player gameplay.

Its biggest weakness is accessibility. The large unit roster, detailed statistics, deck construction, tactical systems, and reliance on battlefield awareness can overwhelm beginners. Players looking for a relaxed RTS with straightforward unit production may find the experience frustrating. The requirement for a third-party EugNet account and internet connectivity is another inconvenience, particularly for anyone hoping to treat it as a completely offline strategy game.

Despite those limitations, Wargame: AirLand Battle remains an impressively deep military strategy game. Its huge unit selection, expansive maps, combined land and air warfare, logistics, dynamic campaign, and large multiplayer battles create a level of tactical freedom that still feels distinctive. It requires patience and rewards players who are willing to study its systems, but successfully coordinating reconnaissance, armor, infantry, artillery, air defense, and aircraft into one effective operation can be immensely satisfying.

Rating: 8/10
